title: Live in an RV, camper or mobile home through a Canadian winter
summary: An RV or mobile home can carry you through a Canadian winter if you keep the water from freezing, the 12 V furnace powered, the vents, exhaust and exits clear of snow, and the air dry. The killers are CO from a blocked exhaust, the generator or the wrong heater, fire, and a flat battery that stops the furnace in the night.

materials.item: Rigid foam board (polyiso or XPS) for windows and skirting
Plywood, vinyl or tarps for skirting
RV antifreeze (propylene glycol), never car antifreeze
Heat tape listed for the pipe, on a GFCI outlet
RV-listed CO/propane alarm and smoke alarm, in date

steps.text: Check every alarm: CO/propane and smoke. Read the dates; MTI's RV CO/propane alarm and Jayco's smoke alarm are good for five years (MTI 25-741, Jayco Alante). Press test, and test weekly while living in it.
steps.warn: The test button checks the horn and circuit, not the sensor (MTI 25-741). Never switch the battery disconnect off with people inside: the alarm goes dead.

steps.text: Open the exit window and make sure everyone can. Keep the ground below it and both exits clear of snow and stored gear (Jayco Alante, USFA RV).

Agree what you do when an alarm sounds. Propane alarm (steady tone) or a smell of gas: everyone goes outside first, then shut the cylinder valve if you can reach it, touch no switches, keep the engine and generator off, and keep the gas off until the leak is found and fixed (Jayco Alante, Dometic AFM). CO alarm (four beeps): everyone into fresh air, count heads, and stay out until it has cleared and the RV is aired out (Jayco Alante, MTI 25-741). Never cut the battery to silence an alarm (Jayco Alante).
Park so the generator exhaust points away and downwind, clear of walls, snowbanks and other vehicles (USFA RV, Onan HDZAA). Bring the slides in.
steps.warn: Never sleep with the generator running unless a CO alarm is working (Onan HDZAA).

steps.text: Read the furnace label for its 12 V draw and work out a night's battery use (notes). Keep batteries fully charged; a flat lead-acid battery can freeze (Victron lead-acid).

Choose dry or wet water. Dry: RV antifreeze in the lines, about 1 cup in each drain trap and the toilet, water from jugs (Winnebago Adinaro, Jayco Alante). Wet: tank heaters on, water heater on, tanks dumped only on days above freezing (Jayco Alante, Winnebago winter).
steps.warn: Only RV antifreeze in the water system; car antifreeze and washer fluid are poisons (Jayco Alante).

steps.text: Fit heat tape straight onto any exposed hose or water line, never over insulation and never overlapped unless its instructions allow (CPSC heat tape). Check it for cracks and charring first.
Skirt the base with foam board, plywood, vinyl or tarps, leaving the furnace exhaust, water heater, fridge vents and generator open. Nothing that burns underneath (Escondido mobile homes).
steps.warn: Boxing in the furnace exhaust or the fridge's low vent can put exhaust or leaked propane into the living space (Dometic AFM, Dometic RM2350). The furnace exhaust can warp or burn what sits in front of it: keep foam, bales and banked snow well clear (Dometic AFM).

steps.text: Cover windows at night with cut-to-fit rigid foam and put covers in the roof vents (Winnebago Adinaro), leaving the exit window and one roof vent free.
Keep propane topped up and the regulator clear of snow and ice (Winnebago winter, Jayco Alante).
Every morning and after every snowfall, clear snow from the furnace, water heater and fridge vents, the generator exhaust, the skirting vents and the exits.

Keep the air dry: with the generator and engine off, crack a roof vent and a window, run the range hood when cooking, open the bath vent when washing, don't dry clothes inside, and wipe windows daily (Jayco Alante).
steps.warn: Generator running: windows and roof vents shut, roof and exhaust fans off, range hood included; open air and fans can pull its exhaust inside (Jayco Alante, Onan HDZAA).

steps.text: Heat with the furnace. Never use the range or oven for heat (Atwood range). Electric heaters only on shore or generator power, 90 cm (36 in) from anything that burns, off when you sleep (Escondido mobile homes).
Rake snow off the roof from a ladder before it builds past about 30 cm (12 in) (Good Sam winter), and check slides and doors for ice before moving them (Jayco Alante).
steps.warn: Don't climb onto a snowy RV roof; work from a ladder with someone footing it.

steps.text: Mobile home: read the data plate's roof snow load (HUD data plate, RDBN mobile homes), keep skirting vents clear (Escondido mobile homes), and check tie-down straps and anchors after freeze-up and thaw (HUD anchors).

notes:
## What you are living in

An RV is a thin box on wheels: single-pane windows, water lines and tanks under the floor, and a propane furnace that won't run without 12 V. A mobile (manufactured) home is better built but has the same weak points: the crawl space, the water line and the roof. Both can carry you through a Canadian winter if you keep the water from freezing, the furnace powered, the vents and exits clear of snow, and the air dry.

## Alarms and the way out

- RV combination CO and propane alarms are wired to the house battery and draw from it all the time; if the battery is disconnected the alarm is dead (Jayco Alante). MTI says nobody should be in the RV with the main disconnect off (MTI 25-741).
- MTI's RV CO/propane alarm is to be replaced after five years and sounds an end-of-life signal; its test button checks the circuit, not the sensors (MTI 25-741). Jayco says to replace the RV smoke alarm within five years too (Jayco Alante). A propane alarm belongs 10–50 cm (4–20 in) off the floor, because propane is heavier than air (MTI 20-441-P).
- These alarms aren't smoke alarms, and the CO alarm may not sound at low levels (MTI 25-741); its four-beep alarm signals CO over 35 ppm (MTI 25-741). See [Carbon monoxide](#guides/safety_carbon_monoxide).
- A combination alarm hangs low in the kitchen area, near the likely propane leaks. MTI recommends a CO alarm in every sleeping area as well (MTI 25-741). The RV alarm is dead whenever the house battery is flat or disconnected (MTI 25-741), so keep a battery-powered CO alarm of your own near where people sleep.
- Look for the rated temperature range on every alarm: MTI's 20-441-P propane detector is rated −35 to 66 °C (−31 to 150 °F) (MTI 20-441-P), and a home CO alarm may not be rated for a cold RV at night.
- Don't trust your nose for propane: age, colds, allergies, tobacco, alcohol and drugs can dull the smell (MTI 25-741).
- The exit window has red latches and an EXIT label. Keep the ground under it solid and clear, and have everyone practise opening it (Jayco Alante). Fire services say to keep doors and windows clear and easy to open, and to practise getting out (USFA RV). In a mobile home, make sure you can get out of each bedroom through a window or escape hatch (Escondido mobile homes).

## The furnace and the battery

RV furnaces burn propane in a sealed box, take combustion air from outside and vent outside, never into the living space or an enclosed porch (Dometic AFM). Never box in the vent.

Dometic's hydro flame AFM furnaces draw 4.2 A (50 W) at 16,000 and 20,000 Btu/h, 7.5 A (90 W) at 25,000 and 30,000, and 11.1 A (132 W) at 34,000 (Dometic AFM); Jayco lists 12 A for the furnace in one motorhome (Jayco Alante). Read your label.

| Furnace draw | Blower runs half of a 12-hour night | Battery used |
|---|---|---|
| 4.2 A | 6 h | about 25 Ah |
| 7.5 A | 6 h | about 45 Ah |
| 11.1 A | 6 h | about 67 Ah |

Add the propane alarm's 90 mA, around the clock: about 2 Ah a day (MTI 20-441-P). In deep cold the battery is often what runs out first (Winnebago Adinaro). These sums assume the furnace runs half the night; in deep cold it runs more, and Jayco warns that more furnace running substantially increases battery draw (Jayco Alante).

When the battery goes flat the furnace stops. It runs on 12 V DC only, its blower and control are part of it, and the burner lights itself; Dometic says never to light it by hand and never to power a DC furnace from a battery charger, even to test it (Dometic AFM). The RV's CO and propane alarm stops with it (MTI 25-741 says it won't work without power and runs down to 7 V). Recharge first, from shore power, a generator placed as below, or solar. Don't fill the gap with the oven, a camp stove or a portable fuel heater: use a sleeping bag in one small space ([Staying warm](#guides/skill_staying_warm)), or move to a heated building if there is one. Keep a spare charged battery.

- Lead-acid batteries hold less in the cold and freeze sooner when they're low, so keep them fully charged (Victron lead-acid). See [Lead-acid batteries](#guides/safety_lead_acid).
- Victron's lithium (LiFePO4) batteries may only be charged between +5 and +50 °C, and lose about 20% of their capacity at 0 °C and 50% at −20 °C (Victron lithium). Plan with [Power budget](#guides/reference_power_budget).

## Water and tanks

Pick one:
- **Dry:** winterize the plumbing with RV antifreeze or compressed air, drink and wash from jugs, and put RV antifreeze down the drains and toilet so traps and tanks don't freeze (Winnebago Adinaro). Jayco says about 1 cup (250 ml) per P-trap (Jayco Alante).
- **Wet:** Jayco's tank heaters protect tanks and lines to about −24 °C (−11 °F), depending on the setup; the big ones are 120 V and do nothing without shore power or a generator (Jayco Alante). Some owners keep the water heater on so it can't freeze and crack, and dump tanks only on days above freezing (Winnebago winter); keep the grey and black valves shut until then (Good Sam winter).

Only RV antifreeze goes in the water system. Car antifreeze (ethylene glycol) and washer fluid (methanol) are poisons (Jayco Alante).

**Heat tape** on a hose or water line: In 1989 CPSC counted about 3,300 residential fires a year involving heat tapes or cables (an old figure; the advice below still holds). Inspect it every fall, and replace it if the covering is cracked or charred or wire shows. Wrap it straight on the pipe, never over insulation, don't overlap it unless its instructions allow, and only insulate over it with non-flammable fibreglass if the maker says so; too much insulation can start a fire (CPSC heat tape).

## Propane

- Propane is the main heat: keep the cylinders topped up (Winnebago winter). The regulator can freeze up, which Jayco counts among the cold-weather risks (Jayco Alante).
- Propane boils at about −42 °C (−44 °F) (NIST propane): the colder it gets, the less pressure is left to push gas to the furnace.
- Furnace fuel use climbs as it gets colder (Winnebago Adinaro). Bringing the slides in leaves less space to heat (Winnebago 10 tips).

## The fridge

On gas, an absorption fridge (the Dometic RM2350 manual lists 230–240 V, so it is a non-North-American model: read this as the general layout and check your own fridge's vents) burns behind a sealed wall: it takes air from a low outside vent, exhausts through an upper vent, and needs a floor-level opening so leaked propane can drain out. Nothing may block that flow (Dometic RM2350). Keep both vents clear of snow, nests and skirting.

## Generator

Generators are a leading cause of CO poisoning in RVs; point the exhaust away and downwind (USFA RV). Walls, snowbanks, brush and other vehicles trap exhaust around the RV, and roof fans or exhaust fans running while the generator runs can pull it inside (Onan HDZAA). Jayco says to keep windows closed while the engine or generator runs (Jayco Alante), so air the RV out for condensation with the generator stopped. Clear drifted snow from the exhaust and from the generator's air inlet and outlet before each start (Onan HDZAA). A portable generator is a separate case: outdoors only, at least 6 m (20 ft) from doors, windows and vents, and open windows or fans don't make it safe indoors (CPSC generators). Never sleep with it running unless the RV has a working CO alarm, check the exhaust for leaks every start and every 8 hours (Onan HDZAA), and turn off auto-start before sleeping unless a working CO alarm is fitted (Jayco Alante).

## Condensation

Two people breathing, cooking and drying things in an RV is a small sealed room ([Condensation and damp](#guides/reference_condensation)). Jayco's advice: crack windows and roof vents, open the bath roof vent about 1 cm (½ in) while showering, run the range hood while cooking or washing up, don't dry towels or clothes inside, prop cupboard and closet doors open, or run a dehumidifier (Jayco Alante). Damp left alone means mould (Jayco Alante); mould starts within 48 hours where things stay wet (Health Canada mould).

## Heat that isn't the furnace

- Never heat with the range or oven: it uses up oxygen and makes CO. Keep a window or vent cracked whenever you cook (Atwood range).
- Winnebago owners advise against catalytic and other fuel-burning heaters and use electric ceramic heaters on shore power or a generator (Winnebago Adinaro). Don't make them the main heat: the furnace ducts also warm the bays and tanks (Winnebago 10 tips). Keep them 90 cm (36 in) from anything that burns, and off when you sleep or go out (Escondido mobile homes).
- Camp stoves, barbecues and outdoor-only propane heaters never go inside: read [Heater labels](#guides/reference_heater_labels).

## Skirting, windows and the roof

- **Skirting** stops wind blowing under the floor (Winnebago 10 tips): foam board, plywood, vinyl or tarps around the base. Leave the furnace exhaust, the water heater, the fridge's low vent and the generator clear. Keep anything that burns out from under a mobile home, straw bales included (Escondido says no combustible material under the home), and keep bales and banked snow off the skirting vents and away from the furnace, water heater and fridge exhaust. Most mobile home furnaces take their combustion air from under the home, so the skirting needs its four to six vents, all kept clear (Escondido mobile homes). A British Columbia regional district, applying the CSA Z240 mobile home standard and the BC Building Code, asks for year-round crawl-space vents, skirting that allows 50 mm (2 in) of frost movement, and no appliance or dryer vented into the crawl space (RDBN mobile homes).
- **Windows** lose most of the heat. Cut-to-fit rigid foam board (polyiso) insulates far better than foil bubble wrap; roof vents lose heat too and take insulated covers (Winnebago Adinaro). Leave the exit window and one roof vent free to open.
- **Snow on an RV roof:** An RV technical advisor writing for Good Sam guesses that the average RV roof can probably take 10–20 lb/ft² (about 50–100 kg/m²), roughly 15–30 cm (6–12 in) of wet snow, and he clears his before it reaches 30 cm (Good Sam winter). That is one writer's rule of thumb with no maker's rating behind it, so treat 30 cm as a ceiling, clear sooner when the snow is wet or heavy, and use your owner's manual if it gives a figure. Rake it off from a ladder; see [Falls](#browse/hazards/fall). Check slides, doors and vents for ice before you move them (Jayco Alante).
- **Mobile home roof:** the data plate near the main electrical panel names the roof load zone it was built for (HUD data plate); US zones are 40, 30 or 20 lb/ft² (HUD roof loads). Mobile homes built to CSA Z240 are marked with their ground snow load and roof design snow load (RDBN mobile homes).

## Mobile home anchors

Tie-down straps and anchors stop a home sliding or tipping in wind. Where the ground heaves with frost, anchor augers have to sit below the frost line (HUD anchors). If an anchor has lifted or a strap has gone slack or rusted through, note it and fix it before the spring winds.
